growth_story.headline: Liberia's income per person, wrecked by war and hit again by Ebola and a commodity slump, has edged up since 2021 but is still below its 1960 level.
growth_story.arc: Liberia's income per person peaked in 1972 and slid through the 1980s, and civil war then wrecked the economy: the 1990 to 1997 era averaged -6.0 percent a year, with income per person bottoming out in 1995. Growth returned from 1998 to 2013 at 3.6 percent a year, despite a sharp fall in 2003 before peace took hold; the World Bank ties the post-war decade to high rubber and iron ore prices, aid and foreign money flowing into mines and plantations. Since 2014 growth has averaged -0.4 percent a year, as the Ebola epidemic, a slump in iron ore and rubber prices, the exit of UN peacekeepers and COVID-19 pushed income per person down through most of 2014 to 2020. Growth has picked up since 2021, led by gold and iron ore mining, but income per person reached only 684 dollars in 2025, still below its 2013 level and below 1960, the first year of the record. Over the last decade it averaged -0.1 percent a year, against 2.6 in the decade before.

threads.title: Civil war and collapse
threads.text: A long decline from the mid-1970s ended in civil war in the 1990s and early 2000s. Income per person fell to its lowest point in 1995, and Liberia lost the middle-income status it once had.

citations.title: Liberia Country Economic Memorandum
citations.quote: From its peak in 1974 to its lowest point in 1995 during the civil war, per-capita income plummeted by an astonishing 93 percent.

citations.title: Liberia Country Economic Memorandum
citations.quote: Real GDP per capita collapsed and Liberia lost its middle-income status.

threads.title: The post-war peace dividend
threads.text: After peace in 2003, high prices for rubber and iron ore, a wave of aid and foreign money into mines and plantations drove a decade of recovery. That growth came from export enclaves that added little at home.

citations.title: Liberia Country Economic Memorandum
citations.quote: driven by surging commodity prices (such as for rubber and iron ore), an influx of foreign aid as part of the “peace dividend,”

citations.title: Liberia Country Economic Memorandum
citations.quote: predominantly fueled by foreign direct investment (FDI), which supported export-oriented production with minimal domestic value addition.

threads.title: A run of shocks after 2014
threads.text: Between 2014 and 2020 a string of blows hit: the Ebola epidemic, falling iron ore and rubber prices, the departure of UN peacekeepers, who had been a key source of foreign exchange and consumer demand, and then COVID-19. Income per person fell in 2019 and 2020 and has not regained its 2013 level.

citations.title: Liberia Country Economic Memorandum

citations.title: Liberia Country Economic Memorandum

threads.title: Mining-led growth with few jobs
threads.text: Recent growth rests on gold and iron ore mining, which has created few jobs. Most workers remain in informal jobs where output per worker is low, so faster output has not meant broad gains.

citations.title: Macro Poverty Outlook: Liberia
citations.quote: Mining expansion has generated few employment opportunities, leaving most workers in low-productivity informal jobs and perpetuating poverty despite headline growth.

citations.title: Macro Poverty Outlook: Liberia

threads.title: Aid cuts and a fiscal squeeze
threads.text: The government cut spending sharply in 2024 to shrink a large deficit, which held growth back. In February 2025 the United States cancelled nearly all its USAID projects, and lower grants have since cut into public investment.

since_last_year.text: In 2025 a surge in gold and iron ore output lifted growth, while farming slowed and lower grants trimmed public investment. In the data, income per person grew 2.8 percent in 2025, its fastest pace since 2013.

growth_story.tension: The sources describe solid, mining-led growth in 2024 and 2025, but in the data income per person rose only 1.8 and 2.8 percent in those years, because the population keeps growing. The World Bank also describes a strong first post-war decade, yet income per person in 2013 was still below its 2000 level, because the collapse of 2003 came first. And the World Bank dates the old peak to 1974, while the data put it in 1972.
